newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open lower before CPI, retail sales.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open lower before CPI, retail sales.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on Thursday before a data troika due in early trade.
At 0830 EST/1330 GMT, the government will release reports on October consumer prices, October retail sales, and jobless claims in the week ended November 9.

A front page story in The New York Times was also cited as a slightly negative influence. In an interview with the newspaper, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said that the Administration would "actively oppose" the adoption of a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced Federal budget.
At 0809 EST/1309 GMT, the 6-1/2 percent 30-year bond was down 7/32 to 100-13/32, yielding 6.47 percent.

The Consumer Price Index (CPI) to be released by the Labor Department shortly is expected to show a 0.3 percent rise for October, according to a Reuters survey, compared to a 0.3 percent increase in September.
The core CPI, the index minus its volatile food and energy items, is expected to be up 0.2 percent after a 0.3 percent September rise.
Retail sales data, to be released by the Commerce Department, are expected to show a 0.3 percent October gain.

That compares with a 0.7 percent increase in retail sales in September. Excluding automobile transactions, retail sales are expected to be up 0.3 percent for October, after a 0.4 percent September increase.
Retail sales have been subdued for months and the market is keenly interested in trying to get a sense of whether consumers are going to return to more robust shopping patterns in the fourth quarter.
At the same time that the market gets the data on retail sales and consumer prices, the Labor Department will release first-time claims for jobless benefits for the latest week.
Economists surveyed by Reuters estimate that 334,000 new claims were filed in the week ended November 9 compared to 331,000 the prior week.

"The Rubin story took us back a little overnight so we'll see how that plays out," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at CS First Boston. "The good news is that we didn't have a lot of time to build up a lot of positive expectations for the budget process, so we didn't have that far to fall," he said.
The market rallied on Tuesday amid optimism that cooperation between the Administration and Clinton could lead to solid progress on balancing the Federal budget.
Alexy said the data to be released at 0830 EST/1330 GMT would be "critical to how the market does today."
He said the report with the most potential "to shake things up" is the retail sales report, then the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and jobless claims, "in that order."
In early trade, three- and six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.03 percent and 5.07 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were up one basis point to 5.14 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 to 100-9/32 to yield 5.72 pct. Five-year notes were down 4/32 to 101-1/32, yielding 6.01 percent.
Ten-year notes were down 5/32 to 102-2/32, yielding 6.22 percent.
